notes.meaning: Solomon took twenty years to complete his two major building projects in Jerusalem. He spent seven years building the temple of the Lord and thirteen years constructing the royal palace. Now that these central works were finished, he turned his attention to other needs across his kingdom.

King Hiram of Tyre had returned these border towns to Solomon because they did not suit his needs. Solomon repaired and fortified the cities, making them safe and useful again. He then moved Israelite families into them to strengthen the northern border of the land.

Solomon led a military campaign north to Hamath-zobah and took control of the region. This is the only military campaign of Solomon mentioned in Chronicles, showing he could defend his borders even though his reign was mostly peaceful. By securing this area on the Orontes River, he kept his kingdom stable and protected against northern threats.

Solomon rebuilt Tadmor, an oasis town in the Syrian desert later known as Palmyra. It sat on valuable trade routes between the Mediterranean Sea and the Euphrates River. He also established store cities in the district of Hamath to supply his troops and safeguard goods.

Solomon fortified Upper and Lower Beth-horon with strong walls, gates, and bars to guard the main pass leading up to Jerusalem. He also built up Baalath and established network centers across the realm to house grain, weapons, chariots, and horses. These extensive construction projects allowed him to defend his empire and display the reach of his rule.

Descendants of the original Canaanite nations still lived in the land because Israel had not wiped them out in earlier generations. Solomon placed these non-Israelite groups under forced labor to carry out his vast building projects. They served as a permanent labor force for the royal works.

Solomon did not make slaves of the Israelites as he did with the Canaanite populations. Instead, Israelites held positions of honor and authority in the royal service. They served as soldiers, commanders, army officers, and leaders of the chariot and cavalry forces.

Solomon appointed two hundred and fifty chief officers to direct and oversee the work force. These supervisors were Israelites chosen to manage the daily labor projects across the kingdom. Their leadership kept the massive building tasks orderly and efficient.

Solomon moved his Egyptian wife from the City of David into a separate palace he had constructed specifically for her. He explained that her living quarters must not be where the ark of the Lord had rested, because that area was holy ground. This relocation honored the sacred history of David's house while giving the queen her own royal residence.

Once the temple was finished, Solomon regularly presented burnt offerings to the Lord on the bronze altar in the temple courtyard. This altar stood right in front of the entrance portico of the sacred building. Having completed the temple structure, he immediately put it to its true spiritual purpose of regular worship.

Solomon followed the law of Moses by presenting sacrifices every single day, both morning and evening. He also arranged special offerings for the weekly Sabbaths, the monthly New Moon festivals, and the three required yearly feasts. True worship was not left to chance, but followed God's appointed rhythm throughout the year.

Solomon organized the priests, Levites, and gatekeepers into regular shifts exactly as his father David had ordered. The Levites led praise and assisted the priests, while the gatekeepers guarded each entrance according to their daily assignments. Solomon respected David as a man inspired by God and obeyed his plans without altering them.

The priests and Levites carefully obeyed every instruction King David had laid down for their duties. They carried out their service faithfully and managed the sacred treasures without departing from the royal orders. Because the leadership honored God's commands, the temple staff followed them willingly.

All the work Solomon set out to do for the temple was successfully finished. The planning, materials, construction, and daily services were now complete in every detail. With the building standing and the worship established, the house of the Lord was fully ready.

Solomon traveled south to the ports of Ezion-geber and Eloth on the shore of the Red Sea in the land of Edom. These coastal towns gave Israel a gateway to southern sea routes and foreign trade. Solomon personally oversaw this new enterprise to expand his nation's commerce.

King Hiram of Tyre provided ships and skilled sailors because the Phoenicians were experts at navigating the open sea. Solomon's men sailed alongside them to the distant land of Ophir and brought back 450 talents of fine gold for the king. This joint trading venture brought immense wealth into Jerusalem to support the kingdom.
